questions.q: According to the framework in this lesson, what is the actual test for whether a workload needs a GPU?
options: Whether the project is broadly described as an 'AI' or 'machine learning' project
Whether the dominant computational cost is large, parallelizable matrix/tensor math — not merely whether the workload is AI-related
Whether the dataset is larger than a few gigabytes
Whether the team already has GPU experience
questions.explain: The real test, grounded in Lesson 1, is whether the workload's cost is dominated by large matrix multiplications that parallelize cleanly across thousands of cores — not a label like 'AI' or 'ML.'

questions.q: Why is traditional ETL (filtering, joining, aggregating rows) generally a poor fit for GPU acceleration?
options: Cloud providers technically prohibit running ETL jobs on GPU instances
ETL always requires more VRAM than any GPU on the market provides
ETL work is fundamentally row-oriented and branchy, not dense matrix math, so a GPU's thousands of simple parallel cores bring little benefit over a CPU
ETL workloads can only run on mainframes, never on cloud VMs
questions.explain: Operations like WHERE clauses and GROUP BY are row-oriented and branchy rather than large dense matrix multiplication, so they don't exercise the parallelism that makes a GPU worth its cost.

questions.q: Why do most classical ML algorithms, such as gradient-boosted trees or linear regression on tabular data, typically run efficiently on CPU rather than GPU?
options: They don't reduce to the kind of large, dense matrix multiplication that justifies a GPU's cost, so CPU implementations are often competitive or faster at realistic dataset sizes
GPUs are physically incapable of running any classical ML library
Classical ML libraries like XGBoost have never been optimized for any hardware
CPUs have more VRAM than any GPU, which is the only relevant factor
questions.explain: Algorithms like gradient-boosted trees and linear models are not dominated by the large matmul pattern that GPUs accelerate, so a GPU's cost premium often isn't justified at realistic tabular dataset sizes.

questions.q: Why is provisioning a GPU instance for a small model served at low inference volume described as a FinOps mistake?
options: FinOps principles only apply to storage costs, never to compute costs
Small models are technically incompatible with GPU hardware and will refuse to run
Low-volume inference is actually impossible to run on any kind of cloud instance

A GPU VM costs meaningfully more per hour than an equivalent CPU VM, and at low request volume there isn't enough sustained parallel load to keep the GPU's thousands of cores busy, so you pay for mostly idle capacity
questions.explain: A GPU instance's premium pricing is only justified when the workload exercises enough of its parallel capacity; low-volume serving of a small model leaves most of that capacity idle, which is exactly the over-provisioning waste FinOps practice flags.

questions.q: What is the risk of forcing a genuinely large training or fine-tuning job onto CPU specifically to save cost?
options: There is no risk; CPU and GPU always produce training jobs of equal wall-clock duration
It always violates the terms of service of every major cloud provider
A job that would finish in hours on a GPU can take weeks on CPU, often costing more overall in wall-clock time and compute-hours combined than the GPU would have
It permanently corrupts the training data
questions.explain: This is the inverse FinOps mistake: avoiding GPU cost on a workload that genuinely needs large-scale parallel matmul throughput can massively extend wall-clock time, often costing more in total than simply using the right GPU instance.
